fatal_errors: The proposed composition is not operationally specified and replaces the equimolar WNbMoTaV coating with an undefined Nb/Mo-containing alloy having intentional Ti addition; in the target system, Ti primarily enters through substrate dilution rather than controlled feedstock addition.
Neither cladding parameters nor wear-test conditions are specified, so the claimed performance under high-contact-stress or extreme-service conditions cannot be reproduced or directly tested.

The boundary claim extrapolates to aerospace and marine extreme service despite the supporting evidence and target measurements being limited to laboratory microhardness and room-temperature reciprocating wear.
explanation: The hypothesis correctly identifies laser cladding of a refractory high-entropy-alloy coating on TC4 as the relevant strategy and predicts increased hardness and reduced wear through a dense, refined, metallurgically bonded microstructure. It also supplies an untreated-TC4 control and an explicit falsification threshold. However, it omits the defining WNbMoTaV composition, powder preparation, 2 mm preset layer, laser-power series, and the optimum near 3.5 kW. It consequently misses the key nonmonotonic process–structure–property relationship involving incomplete melting at low power and over-burning, Ti dilution, and loss of BCC support at high power. The proposed mechanisms overlap only generally with grain refinement and resistance to plastic deformation; lattice-distortion and BCC solid-solution strengthening, Marangoni-driven dilution, and protective tribo-oxide formation are absent. Evidence E2 supports the general feasibility of laser-clad HEA coatings, whereas E1 chiefly concerns corrosion and does not substantiate the wear claims. The experiment is directionally discriminating but lacks fixed processing and tribological conditions, replication/statistical details, and direct comparison among laser powers.
